nameStory: The Maine Snaketail gets its name from its distinctive long, slender abdomen that resembles a snake's body, especially when it curves while the dragonfly is perched. The 'Maine' part honors the state where this species was first discovered and described by scientists. Like other snaketails, it belongs to the clubtail family, named for the slightly swollen tip at the end of their abdomens.
description: The Maine Snaketail is a medium-sized dragonfly with a sleek, streamlined body that's perfectly built for life along New England's rivers and streams. Its body is primarily dark with bright yellow or green stripes running along its thorax (the middle section between head and abdomen), giving it a bold, racing-stripe appearance. The abdomen is long and slender like other snaketails, with a slightly clubbed tip that's characteristic of the clubtail family. Adults typically measure about 2-3 inches long with a wingspan of roughly 3-4 inches.

idTips.label: Snake-like abdomen
idTips.description: The long, slender black abdomen curves gracefully like a snake's body when the dragonfly perches, feeling smooth and segmented if you could touch it

idTips.label: Racing stripes
idTips.description: Bright yellow or greenish stripes run down the sides of the thorax, creating a bold pattern that catches the eye even from a distance

idTips.label: Clubbed tail tip
idTips.description: The very end of the abdomen swells slightly like a tiny club, though less dramatically than some other clubtail species

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are crystal clear with dark veining, making a papery rustling sound when they fly and feeling like thin cellophane

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often perches on rocks, logs, or bare ground near water with wings held perpendicular to the body, rather than folded back

idTips.label: Separated eyes
idTips.description: Large compound eyes don't touch at the top of the head, unlike darner dragonflies, giving them a slightly bug-eyed appearance

habitat: Maine Snaketails prefer clean, rocky streams and small rivers with moderate to fast-moving water, especially in forested areas throughout New England. You'll most often spot them along boulder-strewn waterways where they can perch on sun-warmed rocks between hunting flights. They favor streams with good water quality and are often found in the same areas as trout, indicating the pristine conditions they require.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from streams in late May and early June, looking for sunny spots along the water where they can warm up and hunt for small flying insects.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from mid-June through August when adults are most visible, patrolling territories along streams and engaging in mating flights over the water.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by September, though a few individuals may still be seen on warm days. Eggs laid earlier in the season begin developing in the streambed.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but larvae (nymphs) continue growing under the ice in stream bottoms, buried in sediment and feeding on aquatic insects.

funFact: Maine Snaketail nymphs can spend up to three years living underwater as fierce predators, using an extendable jaw that shoots out like a harpoon to catch prey, before finally crawling out of the water to transform into the flying adult we see for just a few months each summer.
confusionNotes: Maine Snaketails are most easily confused with other snaketail species, but the Maine Snaketail tends to have cleaner, more distinct yellow striping compared to the more muted patterns of Brook Snaketails. Remember: Maine = more vivid markings, like the bold colors of a Maine lighthouse.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being named for Maine, this species is found throughout much of New England and beyond. The name simply reflects where scientists first formally described it, not where it's exclusively found - a common source of confusion with many species names.
compareHints: Compared to its snaketail relatives, the Maine Snaketail has particularly bright and well-defined yellow stripes on its thorax, while Brook Snaketails appear more muted and Riffle Snaketails have more complex patterns. The Rusty Snaketail, as its name suggests, has more brownish coloration rather than the clean yellow-and-black pattern of the Maine species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's snaketails, the Riffle Snaketail is distinguished by its preference for the fastest-flowing water - Maine Snaketails prefer larger rivers, while Brook Snaketails like slower woodland streams.
Brook Snaketails prefer faster-flowing water than most of their snaketail relatives and are typically found in smaller streams rather than large rivers.
